inputs.story:
بنى سور خرساني بطول عمارة خمس أدوار قدام قرية صيد صغيرة، والبحر قدامه هادي زي المراية.
كان عمدة لقرية فيها تلات آلاف شخص بس، وصرف تلاتين مليون دولار و12 سنة بناء على بوابة ارتفاعها 15 متر ونص، مع إن كل القرى اللي حواليه اكتفت بسور 10 متر.
أهل القرية ضحكوا عليه وقالوله: «إنت بترمّي فلوسنا في البحر، الموج عمره ما هيوصل هناك!» بس العمدة ما ردش، ولا نزّل السور سنتي واحد.
السور خلص، والبحر فضل هادي سنين، والناس سمّوه «أغبى مشروع في البلد».
العمدة طلع على المعاش وهو لسه بيتلام على الفلوس اللي ضاعت.
ومات، من غير ما حد واحد يصدقه.
بعد موته بـ 14 سنة، الأرض اتهزت بزلزال عنيف، والبحر اتسحب لورا... ورجع بموجة عملاقة ارتفاعها 15 متر بالظبط!
أصل العمدة وهو شاب شاف البحر بيبلع قريته، فافتكر علامات قديمة على الصخر بتحدد أعلى نقطة وصلها الموج زمان.
زي ما تحط شرطة بالقلم على الحيطة عشان ما تنساش المقاس، هو بنى السور على مقاس أضخم موجة في الذاكرة.
القرى اللي حواليهم بأسوارها الـ 10 متر اتمسحت في دقايق، والموجة خبطت في سوره... ووقفت عند حافته.
القرية كلها نجت، والناس اللي ضحكوا عليه راحوا قبره يشكروه.
inputs.priorities:
What matters most to the owner:
1) Line-by-line coherence: every spoken line gets its matching visual, in the order spoken.
2) The narration WAV is used exactly as-is; the film is exactly as long as the recording (68.08 s).
3) The owner's scene-visualization bible below is his directing reference: follow its 7 scenes, world zones, characters and camera move per beat as the direction for the build.
4) Key props that must read true on screen: the 15.5 m concrete flood gate wall; the 15.5M height marker; the neighbours' 10M wall marker; the 15M wave height marker; the carved mark on the rock; the pencil mark on the wall.
5) Board stills come back for the owner's eye BEFORE any full render.

OWNER'S SCENE VISUALIZATION BIBLE (verbatim):
ملف تخيل المشاهد والإخراج البصري بأسلوب RicksClips3000 (النسخة المعتمدة)
المشروع: قصة السور الخرساني الذي أنقذ قرية كاملة (المدة: 01:08.08 | عمودي 9:16)
الملف الصوتي المعتمد: hady-raie-bhr8740o6.wav
================================================================================

الهوية البصرية وتقسيم العوالم (World Zones & Visual Bible):
- الشخصيات: 2D مسطحة (رأس دائري كبير، عيون نقطية معبرة، جسم حبة فاصوليا، أذرع وأرجل رفيعة، خط خارجي أسود سميك).
  * العمدة (البطل): شعر رمادي قصير، بدلة بلدية داكنة، وقفة مستقيمة ونظرة هادئة ثابتة.
  * أهل القرية / الساخرون: ملابس صيادين وقبعات بألوان دافئة متباينة، تعبيرات مبالغ فيها عند السخرية ثم الصدمة والامتنان.
- تقسيم العوالم (3D Toon Sets):
  * العالم 1 (الساحل والقرية والسور العملاق): قرية صيد صغيرة بمنازل خشبية بسيطة، مرسى قوارب، وسور خرساني رمادي هائل ببوابة فولاذية (15.5 متر) يفصل القرية عن البحر.
  * العالم 2 (ذكريات الشباب + حائط التشبيه): فلاشباك دافئ عتيق لصخرة قديمة على الجبل عليها علامة محفورة لارتفاع الموج + مشهد تشبيه يومي داخل غرفة (حائط وقلم رصاص يرسم شرطة مقاس).
  * العالم 3 (القرى المجاورة ثم مقبرة التل): قرى ساحلية بأسوار 10 متر تغمرها المياه، وتل هادئ يطل على القرية الناجية وفيه قبر العمدة.
- الإضاءة: ضوء شمس دافئ منخفض (ذهبي/برتقالي) مقابل ظلال زرقاء بنفسجية باردة في المشاهد الهادئة، يتحول إلى أزرق رمادي عاصف درامي عند الزلزال والتسونامي، ثم شروق ذهبي دافئ في الختام.

- [00:48.36 - 00:51.61] Close-Up Tracking Along Rock: الكاميرا تتحرك بمحاذاة صخرة قديمة على الجبل محفور عليها خط أفقي واضح (علامة التسونامي القديمة)، ويد العمدة الشاب تلمس الحفر بتركيز.

- [00:58.00 - 01:01.12] Aerial Pan Over Neighboring Towns: لقطة علوية لقرى مجاورة بأسوار 10 متر (ملصق 10M)، تتخطاها الموجة الـ 15 متر بسهولة وتغمرها بالكامل.
- [01:01.56 - 01:03.69] Dramatic Side Profile + Impact Shake: لقطة جانبية سينمائية لسور العمدة (15.5M)؛ الموجة العملاقة تصطدم به بقوة ورذاذ أبيض واهتزاز للكاميرا، وترتفع المياه حتى تلامس الحافة العلوية بالضبط... وتتوقف!
- [01:04.49 - 01:05.22] Smooth Crane Reveal Over the Wall: الكاميرا تعبر فوق قمة السور لتكشف القرية بالخلف سليمة وجافة تماماً تحت شعاع شمس دافئ يخترق الغيوم.

Pass-specific instruction set (build.md from skills/cartoon-shorts/steps):
# Step: Build

**Goal:** turn the member's voice into a film where cartoon characters act every line so well they feel alive, in a lit set with
DEPTH, opening on a character's scared or expressive face. Characters and acting are the heart of it: "perfect character
animation" from a blank script or any character. The set is the previz (the rich set is the Environment overhaul) but it has
depth from the start: the later passes can only add detail and air to the space you give them, and a set that is a wall right
behind the faces stays flat forever.

**Inputs:** `audio/clean.wav` + `audio/clean.json` (the voice and its word times, made by the app), the member's notes, the engine
copy. A SHOT PLAN (binding) in the notes, when there is one, fixes the cuts, places and cameras: follow it segment for segment.

**The bar:** `references/quality-bar.md` and the stills in `references/bar/` (open them first): the space behind the faces, the
practical lights, the faces big. **The guide pages** (`references/guide/`, open the jpg files): 01 the bar, 02 story to shots
(before any scene), 03 the set, 04 characters, 05 the camera grammar, 09 verify, 10 never. Read them before you start and check
your frames against them before you finish. When the project has `references/examples/`, its Build sections show how the bar films
started.

**Made new:** the examples show the method; this film is written from this voice's own words. Never copy an example's film,
acting table, shots, camera or set, even when the voice is the same as an example's: its own cast, its own set in `scenes/set.js`
(or a kit set), its own acting.

**Wide project (16:9):** read `references/wide.md` first. Stage for the width from the first shot and give the set its sides; the rest of this step holds as written.

## Read first
`SKILL.md`, `references/topics.md`, `references/critic.md`, `references/quality-bar.md` (and open the stills in

`references/bar/`), `references/voice-sound.md`, `references/characters.md`, `references/film.md`, `references/camera.md` (the
grammar section), `references/sets.md`, the Build part of `references/pitfalls.md`, and `lessons/build.md` if it exists. Deep
names: `references/api/`.

## Method
1. **Words and the film bible:** read `narration` (or `audio/clean.json`) from 0 to the end. Write the lines as heard (note
   anything that differs from the member's script). Then `scenes/BIBLE.md` by `references/topics.md`: a row per line (speaker,
   place, beat, action word, story prop) and a row per place (the real thing, size in D, far end in D, practicals, colour mood,
   air). Decide everything here first.
2. **Cast:** who says each line, who is the narrator, who else is in the scene. A spec per character in `scenes/cast/<id>.json`
   from a sentence each (or a built-in spec by id). Check each new one on a `render_frames` frame facing the camera and at 3/4.
3. **Set with depth:** the places of the bible in `scenes/set.js` (several places 400 D apart, lights as data, the later passes
   build on it). Each place: the far end 25 D or more from the camera with the camera looking along it, so most shots have space
   behind the characters (a vanishing point helps); 2 or more practicals you can see (lamps, panels, a window) placed along that
   depth. Stage the characters in the space, not against its wall. Keep walking lanes and the camera side clear.
4. **Prove the opening first:** stage, act and light the first shot (the face, the place behind it, its practicals), then run
   the opening critic round (`references/critic.md`) and fix what it names before you act the rest.
5. **Acting:** for every line, the speaker AND the listeners: face first, one body action tied to a word, dead-still holds,
   looks, reactions. Props with owners and hand-overs. Walks that end before the line that needs them.
6. **Camera:** the grammar (camera.md): on the speaker, a cut every 1.5-3 s on a word, low, always moving, faces big. Frame 0 = a face.
7. **Review loop:** `check_preview` -> `film_probe` (shots, PROP GUARD) -> `film_sheet` of the whole film -> `render_frames` on
   faces, actions, feet on the floor and hands on props -> fix the worst thing -> again. Strips on anything fast.
8. **Critic rounds** on the whole film (`references/critic.md`) until the exit list below is true and a critic says YES.
9. **Lessons:** `lessons/build.md` as you go (tried, saw, fixed, still weak), ending with the HANDOVER block (`references/review.md`).

Helper agents for clearly separate jobs (one character's spec, one group's acting, the set) are welcome: each gets the helper
contract of `references/critic.md`, owns its own files, runs in the foreground; `scenes/film.js` stays yours.

## Machine checks
`check_preview` (no load, runtime or film error), `film_probe` (every line and word, PROP GUARD over every frame),
`film_check { kind: 'set' }` (measured and written into the HANDOVER: the Environment overhaul must pass it, Build may not).

## Exit (every line true)
- `scenes/BIBLE.md` is complete (`references/topics.md` section 8).
- The first frame shows a readable, expressive face (head 300 px wide or more on 9:16; `references/wide.md` on 16:9). Talking
  shots: heads 300-430 px; one establishing wide per place: 180-250 px.

   has that these frames lack, worst first.
3. **Work:** change something real, `check_preview`, LOOK (`film_sheet`, `strip` on fast moves, `render_frames` on faces). Fix
   the worst thing radically, at its cause. Again.
4. **Machine checks** of the pass (its step file): every FAIL fixed at its cause. Numbers point, eyes decide.
5. **Critic rounds** (`references/critic.md`): a fresh critic sees your frames shuffled with bar frames and answers in a fixed
   form; you fix the single biggest gap it names; a NEW critic verifies. Repeat until the exit list is true and a critic says
   YES with no blocking fault.
6. **Handover:** `lessons/<step>.md` as you go, ending with the HANDOVER block (`references/review.md`).
Helpers you start get the same standard: `references/critic.md` "Helper contract".

## Hard rules
- **Made new from this voice:** cast, acting, shots, camera and set are written for this film. Nothing taken over from an example.
- **Open on a character's face**, scared or expressive, in the first frame. Never an empty scene, never a back.
- **Pure in t:** every frame is a function of t alone. No `Math.random` (a seeded generator), no `Date`, no state between frames.
- **Never edit the engine copy** (`engine/`, `world/`, `lib/`, `specs/` ...). New looks, sets, props and characters go in `scenes/`.
  If something truly needs an engine change, work around it and write it in your lessons as a gap.
- **Never touch `audio/`.** Voice lines are written as heard.
- **Anything in a place is in every shot of it.** Nothing thin ending at a head. Faces read: within about 60 degrees of the camera, big, never cut by the edge.
- **PROP GUARD:** a prop that jumps on screen fails the film. `pick_up`, `put_down`, hand-overs, place changes on cuts, `snap` on real hits.
- **The set bar** (`film_check { kind: 'set' }`, measured by the app): a shot needs 22 %+ detailed set and at most 80 % flat; the
  film needs a median shot of 28 %+ detail and at most 78 % flat, with no more than 40 % of its shots under. Environment, Post and
  Shading cannot finish below it, and the app's export calls a film below it unfinished.
- **Later passes never change what earlier passes made** unless that is their job: the drawings, the acting, the voice, the shots.
- Stay inside the project. Pictures only through `make_picture` (the member's own setup); never a paid service they did not choose.

## Tools
`check_preview`, `render_frames` (files in `.suite/frames/<batch>/`), `film_sheet { from?, to?, every?, strip?: 'A-B', cuts? }`
(files in `.suite/review/`), `film_probe {}`, `film_check { kind: set|same|calm|flicker|shade_jumps, from?, to?, still?: 'A-B,C-D',
reset? }`, `list_shots`, `narration`, `blender_run { script, args?, timeout_s? }`, `make_picture { prompt, aspect, out, refs? }`,
`tex_job { kind: tiles|decals|sprites|check|sheet, names? }`, `prop_library { search|look|use|stats }`.
Every failure starts `TOOL PROBLEM [<code>]`: `references/tools-sop.md` says what each code means and what to do.
In Bash: `$CZ_PYTHON`, `$CZ_FFMPEG`, `$CZ_FFPROBE`, `$CZ_BLENDER`, `$CZ_NODE`. When one fails: `references/tools-sop.md` (fix or
fetch, retry, never give up on something fixable).

## References (read what the pass needs)
- `references/topics.md`: any script into a film at the bar: the film bible, places in D, numbers per kind of place, worked mini-examples.
- `references/critic.md`: the critic loop, the critic's brief and fixed answer, the helper contract.
- `references/quality-bar.md` + `references/bar/`: what the bar looks like, full-size stills with captions, numbers per kind of place. Every pass.
- `references/guide/` + its `INDEX.md`: the visual guide pages (no / yes frames and the rules per part of production) and the bar

- `references/characters.md`: casting a new voice, specs from a sentence, faces, acting per line, the motion laws, staging for faces.

# Any script, any topic, at the bar: the film bible

The bar films are a submarine, an office maze and a storybook town. A member's voice can be about anything: a diner, a hospital,
a forest, a rocket, a classroom. The bar is the same for all of them: depth behind every face, detail near the lens, light you
can see the source of, air that grows with distance, a colour mood per place, and characters acting every word. This file is
how any script becomes places that can reach that bar. The examples below show the METHOD on unrelated topics; they are never
material to copy.

## 1. Decompose the voice (Build, before any code)
Read `narration` (all of it). For every line write one row in `scenes/BIBLE.md`:
| line | words (as heard) | speaker, listeners | place | beat (what changes) | mood | the action word | the story prop that shows the words |
- A line that names a new place, a new time or a new danger starts a new BEAT. A film over 30 s has 3 or more beats.
- The STORY PROP is the thing that makes the picture say the words: the letter she reads, the 47 scratches, the burnt pie, the
  red button. Without one, a line is two people talking in a room.
- A sound or action word ("BANG", "she slammed", "he pressed") is a one-frame face snap plus a body action on that word.

## 2. Find the real thing, turn it into numbers (one PLACE row each)
For every place, name the real thing it is (a 1950s roadside diner, a hospital corridor at 3 a.m., a lighthouse lamp room in a
storm) and write its numbers before you build:
| place | the real thing | size in D | far end from the main camera (D) | where its depth comes from | practicals you can see | colour mood | air and particles |
- **D = real metres x 1.6** (one D is one head; a door 2.0 m = 3.2 D, an adult's head top 2.6-2.8 D, a seat .55, a counter 1.25).
- **Far end:** at least 25 D (about 15 m) behind the faces in most shots, looked along (a corridor, a street, a window onto the
  outside, a doorway into a lit room, a stair going down). A small real place (a lamp room, a lift, a car) gets its depth from
  a window, a doorway or a stair, never from moving its walls apart until it stops being that place.
- **Practicals:** 2 or more light sources you can see in every place (lamps, a window, a screen, a fire, neon), placed along
  the depth so it falls into pools of light and dark.
- **Colour mood per place** (warm yellow, rusty amber, deep sea teal, cold dawn, cobalt night): you should know where you are
  with the sound off. A place changes its light state when the beat changes the time or the danger.
- **Air per place:** which particles belong there (dust in a closed room, pollen and seeds outside by day, rain, snow, embers,
  steam, fireflies, bubbles) and how much haze (the numbers per kind of place: `references/quality-bar.md`).

## 3. Pick how each thing is made
| what | Build (the previz with depth) | Environment overhaul (the real set) |
|---|---|---|
| the place's shell (walls, floor, ceiling, ground) | a kit set by name or a description object; your own `scenes/set.js` for several places | Blender `build_set.py`: modelled walls with frames, bevels, skirting, sag, seams |
| the hero thing the words name (the diner counter, the lighthouse lamp, the button) | a simple prop in `scenes/props/` at its real size in D | modelled in Blender at hero detail, textured, lit by the place |
| dressing (clutter, plants, signs, tools) | a few kit pieces where the eye goes | Blender scatter + Flow sprites in the ink style + `prop_library` props, organic density (clusters, clear and bad stretches) |
| surfaces | kit colours | Flow tiles at low contrast + decals where dirt gathers |
| sky and the far outside | a kit sky | a painted sky picture (`make_picture`, bottom edge = horizon) with cloud detail |
| light | lights as data, practicals visible | the same rig, the practicals modelled as fixtures |

## 4. The colour script
One look per place and per light state, written in BIBLE.md before any post: "diner noon: bleached warm yellow, hard sun, heat
shimmer; diner night: neon pink and teal, warm counter light, a cold window". One look for the whole film only when the film is
truly one place at one moment.

## 5. Prove one piece first
Before acting the whole film, stage and light the OPENING (the first shot: the face, the place behind it, its practicals) and
run a critic round on it (`references/critic.md`). Every later shot is built from what that proof taught.

## 6. Topic traps (found by walking unrelated briefs through this skill)
- **A big sky** (a desert, a beach, a field, the sea): sky over 40 % of the frame measures as flat set and reads as empty. Paint the
  sky with cloud detail (`make_picture`, bottom edge = horizon), frame the horizon in the upper third, let wires, a sign, birds or
  branches cross it.
- **A night exterior** (a storm, a street, a shore): a black sky and a black sea are a void, not a mood. Clouds lit by the moon or
  the town, waves with foam, wet ground catching the lamps, rain between the lens and the set.
- **A small room whose depth is a window** (a lamp room, a cockpit, a cabin): keep the room's haze low enough that the view through
  the glass keeps its shapes; limit the air by distance or height, and check the window on a with / without pair.
- **A crowd of listeners** (a classroom, a jury, a team): the nearest three or four listeners react 1-3 frames after the trigger
  word; the rest hold dead still. Turn tables and benches so faces look across the lens, never a row of backs.
- **A non-human in a speaking part** (a robot, an animal, a monster): the cast system makes people (`references/characters.md`).
  Build the non-human as a prop in `scenes/props/<kind>.js` that acts as a function of t (a head that turns, eyes or lights that
  snap on the word), give its voice lines to the narrator or a person on screen, and write the choice in `lessons/build.md`.
- **A big bright hall by day** (a gym, a market hall, a station): neither the closed-interior nor the bright-exterior post numbers;
  start between them (quality-bar.md) and write what you ended at in `lessons/post.md`.

## 7. Worked mini-examples (the method on unrelated topics; never copy them)
**A lighthouse keeper's last night (storm, 45 s).** Places: lamp room (real 4 m across = 6.5 D: too small for depth, so the depth
is the storm seen through the glass, 200+ D of sea with the beam sweeping it, and the stair well going down), spiral stair (depth
straight down, 30 D), rocky shore (exterior night, 60 D to the horizon). Practicals: the great lamp, a paraffin lantern, the beam
itself. Story prop: the logbook with its last entry. Colour: lamp room warm amber against cold blue-black glass; shore cold teal,
white foam. Air: rain streaks outside the glass, spray on the shore, dust in the lamp light. Trap: rain particles across a face;
keep them behind the glass or between lens and set, never on the faces.
**The robot at the science fair (bright interior, 60 s).** Places: a school gym (30 x 18 m = 48 x 29 D), the stage end with a
banner, the hallway outside. Depth: look down the length of the gym past the rows of tables, 40 D+. Practicals: high-bay lamps
in a grid, the stage lights, a projector screen. Story props: the robot, the trophy, the volcano model that fails. Colour: high
key, warm gym wood, saturated posters. Air: light haze only (the bright exterior numbers, not the dark interior ones), paper
confetti on the win. Trap: twelve kids at tables read as a crowd of backs; turn the tables so faces look across the lens, and
give every listener a reaction 1-3 frames after the trigger word.
**Grandma's desert diner (noon exterior and a neon night, 50 s).** Places: the road and the diner front (exterior, 80 D to the
mesas), the counter inside (12 m = 20 D, depth through the window onto the road). Practicals: the neon sign, pendant lamps, the
pie case. Story prop: the last slice of pie under its glass dome. Colour: noon bleached warm yellow; night pink and teal neon with
a warm counter. Air: heat shimmer and dust by day, moths round the sign at night. Trap: a sky over 40 % of the frame measures as
flat set; paint the sky with cloud detail and frame the horizon in the upper third with the sign and wires crossing it.
**The night nurse (dark interior, 40 s).** Places: a hospital corridor at 3 a.m. (40 m = 64 D), the nurse station, one ward.
Depth: the corridor itself, looked along. Practicals: ceiling panels every 5 D, the station's desk lamp, monitor glow, an exit
sign. Story prop: the call light above bed 7. Colour: cold green-white corridor, warm station. Air: the dark interior numbers,
fine dust. Trap: even ceiling light everywhere reads flat; break it into pools (every second panel dimmed, one that flickers on
a beat) so the faces move through light and dark.

## 8. Before you hand the bible on
- Every line has a place, a beat, an action word and a story prop.
- Every place has its real thing, size in D, far end in D, 2+ practicals, a colour mood and its air.
- The opening's place is staged, lit and proven by a critic round.
The Environment overhaul's contract (`scenes/ENV_CONTRACT.md`) starts from this bible: per place what it must become.
# The critic loop: you never grade your own work

Your own checks pass things a fresh critic rejects at first look. So every pass ends with critic rounds: a NEW agent that never saw
your reasoning looks at your frames next to the bar, answers in a fixed form, and you fix the one biggest gap it names. Then a
new critic verifies. The checks (`film_check`, `film_probe`, PROP GUARD) are the floor; the critic is how you get from the floor
to the bar.

## When
| stage | critic rounds on |
|---|---|
| Build | 1. the OPENING (0 to the end of the first shot) as soon as it is staged and lit, before the rest of the film is acted: the first face, the depth behind it, the light; 2. the whole film at the end of the pass |
| Camera angles | the whole film at the end (strips of the fast moves go in the picture set) |
| Environment overhaul | each place when its tracks have landed, then the whole film at the end |
| Add post processing | the whole film at the end, one picture per place at least |
| Shading pass | the whole film at the end, faces of every place |
The director (Berserk or the member) reviews between passes as well; that never replaces your critic rounds.

## A round, step by step
1. **The pictures.** Render the moments the critic must see at full size: `render_frames` at `scale: 1` on the opening frame, one
   moment per place, every moment this pass changed most, and any moment the last report named (6 to 10 pictures; the files land
   in `.suite/frames/<batch>/`, the newest folder). Strips of fast moves come from `film_sheet { strip }` (`.suite/review/`).
2. **Blind mix.** Take the same number of bar pictures: the bar tiles of this pass's pages (`references/guide/INDEX.md` lists them,
   in `references/guide/tiles/`) and stills from `references/bar/*.jpg`. Make every picture, yours and the bar's, the same size so
   size and shape give nothing away: `"$CZ_FFMPEG" -y -i <in> -vf "scale=600:800:force_original_aspect_ratio=increase,crop=600:800"
   <out>.jpg` (the guide tiles already are 600x800). Put them into `.suite/critic/r<N>/` under neutral names `p01.jpg`, `p02.jpg`
   ... in a shuffled order. Write which is which into `.suite/critic/r<N>.key.txt`. The critic never reads the key, your lessons, your notes
   or this conversation. A crop hides the frame's edges: put the full frames (`render_frames` at `scale: 1`) next to the crops when
   the round is about framing, and say so in the brief. On a wide (16:9) project the crops hide the shape too; the blind score
   still counts.
3. **Start the critic** (one helper agent, in the foreground, a new one every round) with the brief below, filled in. In the
   Environment overhaul the crew has a named `critic` agent for this; in the other passes start a general helper.
4. **Read its answer.** Save it as `.suite/critic/r<N>.report.md`. Count how many of the bar pictures it took for yours and how
   many of yours it took for the bar: write both numbers in your lessons (the blind score).
5. **Fix only the BIGGEST GAP**, at its cause, radically (one cause, one change, so the next round shows what it did). A BLOCKING
   fault the critic marks as a one-line fix (a cropped face, a jumping prop, a frame inside a head) may ride along.
6. **Next round** with a NEW critic: the same moments again plus anything the fix touched, and the last report, so it can say
   what is fixed.
7. **The pass is done** when its step file's exit list is true AND a critic answers `VERDICT: YES` with no BLOCKING fault.
**The same fault twice:** when a new critic names the same fault after your fix, the fix was the wrong kind: change the method,
not the amount (geometry or a modelled piece instead of a texture, a real light instead of a brighter grade, another camera
position instead of a nudge, a new sprite or Blender piece instead of a decal). Never answer a critic by turning an effect down
until it is gone, by cutting a beat, a character or a set piece, or by loosening a number.
**Faster builds on** (the request says so): one critic round at the end of the pass; fix every BLOCKING fault it names.

## The critic's brief (paste it, filled in, as the helper's whole prompt)
```
You are the CRITIC of one pass of a 3D cartoon short (Creatorize, 3D Cartoon Shorts (New)). You never write or edit a file and
never build anything: you look and judge, and you are hard to please. The bar: a stranger watching on a phone would not guess a
tool made it.
Open EVERY picture in <project>/.suite/critic/r<N>/ with Read. Some are frames from the bar films, some are from the film under
review; you are not told which. Judge every picture on its own against the rules below.
THE PASS: <Build | Camera angles | Environment overhaul | Add post processing | Shading pass>, its job: <one line from SKILL.md>.
RULES FOR THIS PASS: <paste the step file's "Exit" list and the six look questions of references/review.md>.
DO NOT FAULT (outside this pass's job): <for example, in Camera angles: the set's detail, the post, the shading>.
THE LAST REPORT: <paste it, or "none">.
Answer in exactly this form, nothing else:
VERDICT: YES | NO
BIGGEST GAP: <one sentence: what, in which picture, what the bar pictures show instead>
FAULTS (at most 5, ranked by how much fixing each lifts the film):
1. BLOCKING | MINOR  p<NN>  <the fault in one sentence>  <a number against the bar: "head 180 px, bar 300-430 px",
   "far end about 3 D behind the faces, bar 25 D+", "faces flat white, no shadow colour">  FIX: <one concrete change>
LAST REPORT: <each of its faults: fixed | not fixed | worse>
WHICH ARE THE FILM'S: <the picture ids you think come from the film under review>
BLOCKING = a viewer would see a tool made it, or a hard rule breaks: no face in the first frame, a frame inside a head or wall,
a back on a speaker, a face cut by the edge, a flat white or mud face, a wall a metre behind the faces, a prop that jumps, an
empty or flat set, a character that does not move on its line. MINOR = below the bar, the shot still reads.
```

## The helper contract (any agent you start: a part builder, a track of the environment crew, a critic)
Every brief carries, in this order:
1. **The goal** of its part in one or two sentences, and the feel.
2. **The bar:** "read `references/quality-bar.md`, open the stills in `references/bar/` and the guide pages of this pass
   (`references/guide/`, named in the step file), and compare your result with them at full size before you report".
3. **What must hold** (the pass's "What must hold"), **the files it owns** (one writer per file) and the files it must never touch.
4. **Its tools** and `references/tools-sop.md` for failures.
5. **Its exit:** the numbers and checks its part must pass before it reports, and "nothing leaves you below the bar: a target
   you cannot reach is reported with the reason, never skipped".
6. **Its report:** what it made, the files, the numbers it reached, what is still below the bar (worst first), and any change it
   needs in a file that is not its own.
Never in a brief: a clock, "keep it quick", "good enough", "a complete set on time beats a perfect one", "if there is time".
When the member turned on Faster builds, say so in the brief and pass on the FASTER BUILDS block word for word.
# The quality bar: what "at the bar" looks like

Films set the bar for this style. The owner called S-4 "borderline insane" and the backrooms film "Flawless, this is perfect";
The Town Built Around a Button (65 s, 35 shots, 19 characters, a walled town by day and night and a field) is the bright,
exterior proof that the same bar holds far from a submarine or an office maze. Full-size stills are in `references/bar/`
(`s4_*.jpg`: a sunken submarine, `backrooms_*.jpg`: a yellow office maze), each set with a caption file (`s4.md`,
`backrooms.md`) that says what makes each frame good. Some projects carry only one of the sets: use what is there. The guide pages
in `references/guide/` show no / yes frames per part of production, many of them from the Town film (`references/guide/INDEX.md`).

**Open the stills at the start of every pass, before your "before" frames.** At the end, put your own frames next to them at
full size (`render_frames` with `scale: 1`) and run the critic rounds (`references/critic.md`). A pass is done when, frame for
frame, nothing big the bar has is missing from yours AND a fresh critic says YES. The checks passing is NOT done: checks only
say nothing broke. They never say it looks good.

The stills are the bar for the LOOK, never material: this film's set, cast, shots and colours come from its own story
(`references/topics.md`).

## What the bar has that a first try lacks
A first try usually "works": every check passes and the picture is flat. These are the gaps the owner sees at once.

| | the bar | a first try |
|---|---|---|
| depth | the set goes on behind the characters: a corridor, a room, a street, a horizon with a far end 25 D+ away, often a vanishing point near the middle of the frame | characters lined up against a wall a metre behind them |
| near detail | modelled things close to the camera and at frame edges (pipes, door frames, crates, rails, ceiling grid, a hedge, a lamp post) that frame the faces | empty floor and blank wall |
| ceiling and floor (or ground and sky) | ceilings with tiles, panels, pipes, chains; floors with stains, rugs, debris; outside: cobbles, kerbs, grass clumps, a painted sky with clouds | flat planes, a gradient sky |
| lights | practicals you can see (panels, lamps, a lantern, lit windows) that light the set and the faces around them, pools of light and dark | even light everywhere, no visible source |
| air | haze that grows with distance so far things fade, light hanging in the air near lamps, dust, pollen or bubbles that drift | a clear, sharp picture to the far wall |
| focus | sharp characters, background softly out of focus (depth of field), bokeh on far lights | everything equally sharp |
| faces | lit by the scene: a warm (or cold) key from the lamp or sun side, a darker coloured shadow side, a rim in the backlight | flat white or flat grey discs |
| grade | one strong colour mood per place and light state (warm yellow, rusty amber, deep sea teal, cold dawn, cobalt night), a vignette | neutral colours, no vignette |
| places | each place has its own light and grade; the change on a cut tells you where you are | one look for the whole film |

## The measured floor (the app's set bar, `film_check { kind: 'set' }`)
Per shot: 22 %+ of the frame is detailed set and at most 80 % is flat (fog, void, a bare wall, a gradient sky). The film: a median
shot of 28 %+ detail and at most 78 % flat, and no more than 40 % of the shots under the shot line. The Town film measures 63 %
detail / 42 % flat; S-4 38-56 % / 49-67 % across its passes; a member film of grey fog and plain boxes measured 16 % / 86 %. Passing it is the floor,
not the bar.

## Numbers per kind of place (to calibrate, never to copy)
Start from the row that matches the place, then tune by eye next to the stills. The same numbers on another kind of place are a
mistake: the dark-interior haze and aperture turned the bright Town into a grey-white veil and blurred the button in the
foreground, until the haze was halved, `far` came down to 70-90 and the aperture to 9.
| kind of place | air (haze) | depth of field | bloom | particles | grade |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| dark interior (S-4 torpedo room, backrooms) | density about .03 (haze clearly visible at 10 m), light in the air .25-.3 | aperture 26-30 | about .3 above .75 | 1,000+ slow dust motes | gamma .84, contrast 1.12, a colour tilt, vignette |
| underwater | denser (.034), moving light shafts | aperture 26-30 | on the lights | bubbles, marine dust | deep teal, vignette |
| bright exterior by day (the Town) | density about .0055 from 8 D out, `far` 70-90 so the sky keeps its colour | aperture 9, nearK .22 | light | pollen, seeds (size about .010) | gamma 1.10, saturation 1.28, vignette |
| exterior at night (the Town's night years) | coloured haze (cobalt), the lamps' light hanging in it | aperture 9 | warm bloom on every window and lamp | fireflies, snow or petals as the story's season wants | cooler than the day (the Town: gb 1.06-1.15), vignette |
| a macro close-up of a prop | no haze | none or very light: the prop is the subject | on its highlights | a little dust | crisp: gamma up, contrast up |
| a big bright hall by day (a gym, a market hall; no film measured yet) | between the closed interior and the bright exterior: about half the interior density, `far` set to the hall's length | aperture 12-20 | on the windows and lamps | dust in the sun shafts | warm or neutral, vignette |
A pass that ends far below its row (haze .002 in a dark interior, bloom .14, 200 specks, no vignette) has turned its effects off,
not tuned them.

## Fixing without losing the effect
When an effect causes a problem (haze washes out the sky, rays make blotches, a grade turns faces muddy), fix the cause (limit it by
height, distance or place, keep it off the faces, move the light) and keep the effect. Turning an effect down to nothing is not a fix.

## How you know a pass skipped something
Its lessons show no "before" frames, no critic round, no frames next to the bar stills, or a HANDOVER with nothing below the bar.
Every real pass has all of them.
# Voice and sound

## The voice is made by the app
- `audio/clean.wav` = the member's voice, already trimmed with no gaps (a 15 ms buffer around each cut).
- `audio/clean.json` = its word times. `audio/timeline.json` = the app's timeline. Never edit, trim, re-time or replace these files.
- Read the words with `narration` (or open `audio/clean.json`). Film time = the voice's clock: t = 0 is the first sample of `clean.wav`.
- In `scenes/film.js`: `voice: { file: 'audio/clean.wav', words: 'audio/clean.json', lines: [...] }`.

## Lines
- Split the words into `lines` in order, one line per speaker turn (or per sentence for a narrator). Each line's `text` must give
  exactly the words in `audio/clean.json`, in order (case and punctuation ignored). Leftover or missing words stop the film and name the line.
- **Write them as heard.** The read can differ from the script ("fights its way" was in the read, not the script). Use the read and
  say so in your notes; never silently "fix" it.
- `!` at the end of a word = a shout (the big open mouth). `loud: true` on a line = every word. Only on real shouts.
- If the words look wrong (a name heard as another word), the member can fix the transcript in the app; say so in plain words.

## Times tied to words
Every time key takes `'line:N.start'`, `'line:N.end'`, `'line:N.word:K'`, `'line:N.word:K.end'`, each with `+0.2` / `-0.3`.
Tie acting, props and cuts to words, never to raw seconds: the times stay right when the member trims the voice again.

## Sound
- The app does the sound design automatically (effects from the film's actions and cuts) and the mix. Music is added by the member
  by hand in the app. This style has no separate sound step: do not write mix scripts or sound files.
- Help the automatic sound: clear actions on words (a knock, a drop, a door) and cuts on hits give it something to land on.
- If the camera pass moves the cuts, the app's sound design follows the new cuts on its next run; mention in your notes any sound
  that was tied to an old cut.
# Characters: specs, faces, wardrobe, acting

The characters are the heart of the style. 2.5D cartoon people: round white heads, bold ink outline, stick limbs, egg torsos,
faces made of curves that snap between drawings. One JSON spec each. Deep reference: `api/BODY_API.md`, `api/WARDROBE_API.md`,
`api/FACE_API.md`, `api/MOTION_API.md`.

## Casting a new voice
1. Read the words (`narration`, or `audio/clean.json`). Decide who says each line. Lines nobody in the scene says are the narrator
   (`who: null`): no lip sync, the captions still show them. A story told in the first person usually has the teller on screen.
2. One character per speaking role, plus only the extras the story needs (each extra is in every shot of that place).
3. Give each a sentence (age, build, clothes, one owned colour, one thing that tells them apart), then turn it into a spec with the
   table below. Lead characters get 3-6 torso details, extras 1-3.
4. Stage them for faces before you write any acting: where each stands, which way they cheat to the camera, who is in which place.

## A character from a sentence
Start from the closest built-in spec in `specs/` (engineer, boss, mara, walter, pip, nurse, chef, dotty, postman, ruby, bouncer and
more: list the folder) and write `scenes/cast/<id>.json`. Read the sentence in this order:
| words | key | value |
|---|---|---|
| slim, lanky / average / stout, chubby / curvy | `torso.body` | `{ build: 'slim', W: .60-.72 }`, `medium` .75-.87, `stout` .90-1.0, `curvy` |
| kid / teen | `torso.body.build: 'kid'` + `limbs.legLen` .72, `armLen` .62 / teen legLen ~1.08 | never scale the head |
| tall / short | `limbs.legLen` 1.42-1.45 / 1.1-1.15 | always write `legLen` and `armLen` (.9-1.0) |
| shirt, blouse, jumper, vest, jacket, coat | `torso.outfit.layers[]` innermost first | `{ t: 'shirt', color: '#hex' }` |
| apron, tie, bowtie, scarf, belt, buttons, pocket, suspenders | after the garment they sit on | colours always `'#hex'` |
| stripes, tartan, tweed, dots | `pattern` on one garment | one pattern per character |
| skirt, dress | `torso.outfit.skirt` | `{ color, length: 'knee' \| 'ankle', shape: 'aline' \| 'bell' }` |
| trousers, jeans | `torso.outfit.trousers` | the band colour (`'#3f5a86'` jeans) |
| hair | `hair` | `{ style: bald, bald_sides, receding, short, side_part, curly, bob, long, bun, ponytail, pigtails, messy, spiky, colour }` |
| beard, moustache | `facialHair` | `{ kind: full, goatee, stubble, moustache, walrus, handlebar, mutton, colour, scale }` (full beard scale .66-.8) |
| glasses | `glasses` | `{ kind: round, square, half, sun, cateye, oval }` |
| hat | `hat` | `{ kind: ballcap, flatcap, beanie, headscarf, strawhat, chef, bowler, tophat, officer, headband, none }`. No hat = `'none'` |
| big eyes, heavy brows | `face` | `eyeSize` .97-1.04, `browThick` 1.3-1.5 on a lead |
Then the unsaid things: no two main characters share hat type AND colour, one strong owned colour each, 3-6 torso details for a lead,
1-3 for crowd. Never noses, ears, fingers, skin tones, a bigger or smaller head, gloves, boots. Under a hat use short hair.
Check a new character with `render_frames` on a frame where it faces the camera and one at 3/4: silhouette tells him apart, face
and glasses on the head, beard inside the outline, no hair above a hat.

## Faces (they snap, never tween)
`face` keys: `{ t, eyes, brow, mouth }` or `{ t, expr }`.
- eyes: `open smug half blink arc wide wince angry sad look_l look_r stare pinpoint`
- brow: `on off up down knit worried quizzical`
- mouth: `rest smile frown smirk D crescent grid o wide flat tight gulp` (+ visemes, automatic while talking)
- `expr` presets: `fear terror dread gulp confused relief hope dawning horror stare blank`. A preset key does not trigger the
  automatic body reaction: add `react: 'recoil'` or write the fields out.
Talking is automatic (lip sync, small mouth, brow on the stressed word). Listeners are automatic too: a blink, a brow or an eye swap
after each other speaker's line, and their pupils follow the speaker. Your face keys carry the story on top of that.
The engine holds each eye or brow state at least 8 frames. `{ eyes: 'arc', hold: true }` keeps a closed-eye smile.

## Acting per line (the heart of it)
For every line, the speaker AND the listeners:
1. **Face first:** the speaker's expression at `line:N.start-0.1`; a listener's reaction 1-3 frames after the trigger word (`+0.07`).
2. **One body action per line, tied to a word**, one frame after the face (`+0.03`), then a dead still hold. Every arm move gets an
   end: `hold` (seconds) + `out` (frames back), the next clip on that arm, or a hand-over.
3. **Strong reactions:** a face key with new `wide` / `wince` / `angry` / `sad` eyes also moves the body 2 frames later (recoil, jolt,
   lean, slump). `react: false` for a deadpan beat.
4. **Look:** `look: [{ t, at: [x, headY, z] }]` at the other person but 2-3 D toward the camera from them, or the face turns to
   profile and vanishes. Look at the thing 1-3 frames before the reaction face. Keep low targets near eye height (y 1.3-1.6).

| the script says | clip (params) |
|---|---|
| hello, bye | `wave` (`side`, `eyes: 'arc'`) |
| angry, impatient | `akimbo` (`side: 'both'`) + an angry face |
| don't know | `shrug` |
| confused, oh no | `hand_to_temple` |
| there, you, offer, reach | `point` (`side`, `dir: [x, y, z]` body space, +X = his left; keep z <= .3) + `hold`, `out: 6` |
| surprise | `shock_pop` or `shock_jump` (`hold: .1, out: 5`) |
| pain, cringe | `wince` |
| excited | `hop_bounce` (camera still) |
| leans in / recoils | `lean_over` / `lean_back` |
| drinks / eats | `sip` / `eat` (the prop already in that hand) |
| picks up / puts down | `pick_up` / `put_down` (`prop`, `side`; stand within ~.75 D) |
| carries, shakes, signs | `carry`, `shake`, `sign` |
| grabs a collar | `grab_collar` (`target`, stand 1-1.2 D apart) |
| hits, knocks | `knock` (a hit frame the PROP GUARD allows) |
| glasses off / on | `glasses_lower`, `glasses_off`, `glasses_on` (spec glasses only) |
| turns, looks fast | `turn` (`by`), `head_turn` (`yaw`) |
| sits / stands | `sit_on` (a key, not a clip: walks to the seat and sits), `sit_down`, `stand_up` |
Talking hands: `talk_hands` (`dur` = the line) on one line in three at most.

## Walking, heights, places
- `walk: [{ t0, path: [[x, z], ...], speed, face, gait: 'run' }]`. speed ~1.3 stroll, 2.6 normal, 3.5+ brisk. Time a walk to END
  before the line that needs him. Exits in 3/4: never more than ~10 frames of a back.
- `height`: `[{ t: 0, y: 6 }, { t: 'line:1.word:3', y: 0, over: 2.2 }]` floats then sinks; `{ t, fall: 0 }` falls and lands;
  `legs: 'tread' | 'float' | 'climb'`. The world does not collide: build the deck at the height you write.
- `place: [{ t: 'line:5.start', at: [400, 1], ry: 70 }]` + a shot starting at the same time = he is elsewhere after the cut, prop in
  hand, no copy in the cast. A place key mid-shot is a teleport on screen.

## His laws (the motion)
On ones, no motion blur. Three speeds: face snaps (0 in-betweens), gestures 2-4 frames then stop, body moves ~10 frames with most
of it done by frame 4-5. Impacts stop dead. Holds are DEAD still: no breathing, no idle sway; life comes from the face and the
camera. Face first, body one frame later, head leading. No nods while talking.

## Staging for faces
The face draws only while the head is within ~95 degrees of the camera; past that only the back of the hair shows. Keep speakers
within 20-60 degrees. Two people talking: 1.5-1.8 D apart, both cheated 45-70 degrees toward the camera side. Never open on a
character from behind, even when the script says "her back turned": start her 3/4 and let it play in her eyes.
# The film format (`scenes/film.js`)

One file: `export default { ... }`. It may import its own modules (`./shots.js`, `./post.js`, `./shade.js`) and compute tables:
one table of hits can drive the hands, the props and the camera together. The page resolves it the way the engine's film maker
does, then draws frame t. Film time = the voice's clock. The full reference is `api/FILM_API.md`
(written for our own tools: its `films/<film>/` is your `scenes/`, its `make_film` is the app's preview and render). If a name here is
wrong, the deep docs in `api/` (FILM, MOTION, FACE, BODY, WARDROBE, WORLD) win.

## Skeleton
```js
export default {
  fps: 30, size: [1080, 1920],
  world: { set: 'own', setOpts: { } },                 // or a kit set name: 'park', 'kitchen', 'plain' ... (sets.md)
  cast: { maya: { spec: 'cast/maya.json', at: [-1.2, 0.8], ry: 30 } },
  voice: { file: 'audio/clean.wav', words: 'audio/clean.json',
           lines: [ { who: null, text: 'If you ever find yourself here' }, { who: 'maya', text: "Don't, that's Lena" } ] },
  acts: { maya: { face: [ { t: 0, expr: 'fear' } ], clips: [ ], look: [ ], walk: [ ] } },
  props: [ ], handovers: [ ],
  shots: [ { t0: 0, t1: 'line:2.start', camera: { move: 'push', from: { pos: [0.5, 2.3, 9], target: [-1.2, 2.5, 0.8] },
                                                   to: { pos: [0.3, 2.3, 7.5], target: [-1.2, 2.5, 0.8] } } } ],
  captions: 'words',
};
```

## Keys
| key | what |
|---|---|
| `fps`, `size` | 30, `[1080, 1920]` (9:16) or `[1920, 1080]` in a wide project (`wide.md`). The project's format decides |
| `world` | `{ set, setOpts }`. `set`: `'own'` = `scenes/set.js`; a kit set name; or a description object (sets.md). `setOpts` = the set's knobs and the post / shading settings |
| `cast.<id>` | `{ spec, at: [x, z], ry, y, face }`. `spec` = a built-in id in `specs/`, `'cast/<id>.json'` (your file), or an inline object. `ry` 0 faces +Z (the camera side), 90 faces +X. `y` = stands on a deck that high |
| `voice` | `{ file, words, lines: [{ who, text, loud }] }`. `who: null` or not in the cast = narrator (no lip sync; captions still show it) |
| `acts.<id>` | the character's timeline: `face look clips walk sit_on height place blink plants base` (characters.md) |
| `props` | `[{ id, kind, owner, in, at, rot, keys, ...opts }]`. `in`: `'hand:R'`, `'hand:L'`, `'body'`, `'world'`, `'hidden'` |
| `handovers` | `[{ prop, from, to, t, fromSide, toSide }]`: both hands meet, the prop changes hands on screen |
| `shots` | `[{ t0, t1, camera, seam, hard, focus, still }]`, hard cut at each `t0` (camera.md) |
| `captions` | `'words'` = one or two big bold words per beat (his style); `true` = the spoken line in the lower third |
| `endHold`, `endFrame`, `drift`, `lowCams` | the ending is automatic (.5 s after the last word or action); `drift: false` = authored cameras only |

## Voice lines and times tied to words
- The words in `audio/clean.json` are split across `lines` in order by matching each line's words (case and punctuation ignored).
  A mismatch or leftover words stops the film and names the line. So write each line exactly as it was spoken: `narration` shows it.
- Any time key takes a word time: `'line:N.start'`, `'line:N.end'`, `'line:N.word:K'` (word start), `'line:N.word:K.end'`, each with
  `+0.2` / `-0.3`. N and K count from 1. Works in `acts`, `props`, `handovers`, `shots` (incl. `parkAt`, push `t0`/`t1`, `sit_on.t0`).
- A clip's `at` is read only when it is a `line:` string. Seconds go in `t0`: `{ clip: 'wave', t0: 2.2 }`.
- **Loud words:** talk is a small mouth. A word ending in `!` in `text` gets the big open mouth; `loud: true` on a line = every word.
  Put `!` only on real shouts.

## Props
- Built-in kinds: `mug cane loaf half_loaf newspaper box pen camera umbrella phone book bag ball cup bottle broom fishing_rod flowers
  letter` (+ more in `engine/props/`). Anything else: `scenes/props/<kind>.js`, `export function build(opts) -> Object3D`, origin at
  the grip. Give props print and state (a title, a headline, `open`), never a blank slab.
- One owner on every frame. Owner changes move the prop on a short path, never a pop: `pick_up`, `put_down`, `handovers`.
- Opts over time: `{ t: 'line:3.end+0.5', open: 1, ease: 0.2 }` changes the prop's build opts from `t`.
- Falling: `{ t, drop: { from: [x, y, z], v0: [vx, vy, vz], ground: 0, hide: true } }`. Always give `from`.
- A prop that hides itself: hide an inner group (the stage sets the prop's own `visible` every frame).
- Hiding a prop inside a shot, or making it appear in a hand inside a shot, stops the film: do it on a cut, or with `stow: true` /
  `fetch: true` on the key.

## Shots in short (camera.md has the rest)
`move`: `park { pos, target, fov }`, `push { from, to, t0, t1, ease }`, `orbit { who, az0, az1, el, dist, height, fov }`,
`follow { who, camOffset, look, parkAt }`, `path { keys: [{ t, pos, target, fov, roll, shake, walk, stop }] }`. Any camera takes
`roll` (degrees, or `[r0, r1]`). `pos` / `target` on a path key also take `{ who, offset }`, `{ whos: [a, b], offset }`,
`{ object: 'name', offset }` (a set object by `.name` or `set.points`) and `{ prop: 'id', offset }`.
A shot's `focus` names what depth of field keeps sharp (a character or prop id). `seam: true` = a hidden cut (judged by the guard);
`hard: true` = a real cut the guard should not judge.

## PROP GUARD
Run `film_probe` to get its verdict (it also prints the framing of every shot). Each frame it asks how far each prop moved as this frame's camera
sees it. Over 40 px is reported; a move fails the film when it is a real jump (much bigger than its neighbours). Allowed: an impact
(a clip with a hit frame, like `knock`; a clip entry `snap: 6` or `[6, 14]`; a prop key `snap: true`), a placement key's travel,
anything across a hard cut. Camera flights do not count.

## Grade
With the post pipeline on (post.md), the grade is part of the post settings per place and the page draws it, so the preview shows it.
Without it, a top-level `grade: { vignette, places: [{ name, windows, gamma, contrast, saturation, gr, gg, gb }] }` is the film's one
grade. Never both.

## Tool details
- `check_preview`: run after every edit of film.js, set.js, props or settings. A film error names the key path, for example
  `"line:9.end" at shots[3].camera.parkAt: no line 9`.
- `render_frames`: frames at given times, full size. Use them for faces, contact, framing, a set detail.
- `film_sheet`: every 3rd frame tiled with frame numbers, a yellow bar on each shot's first tile. `strip` = a range at full frame
  rate (check every fast move: a camera can pass through a head between sampled frames). `from` / `to` for a range.
- `film_probe`: the resolved film (`.suite/resolved.json`), one line per shot (times, camera move, the words in it), the cast, lines
  and words, and the PROP GUARD verdict over every frame. Run it after every change to props, hands or shots.
- `film_check { kind }`: numbers, no pictures. `same` (characters, props, shots and voice against the start of this step), `calm`
  (light jumps while the camera is still, `still: 'A-B'`), `flicker` (brightness jumps off the cuts), `shade_jumps` (the shading
  formula per face per frame). Faces, feet and hands have no number: look. See review.md.
- Hot reload: the preview reloads on any change under `scenes/` or `assets/`. A page loads textures once at its start: render
  only after the asset folders have gone quiet.
# Camera

The camera is where the film gets its feel. The Build pass shoots it plainly and well (the grammar below); the Camera angles pass
rewrites only `shots` from an instruction set (`cameras/`). Acting, props, voice and captions stay identical between camera versions.

## The grammar (Build pass default)
1. The camera is on the SPEAKER while a line is spoken. Cut to a listener only for a reaction beat, then come back.
2. Cut every 1.5-3 s, on a line start (`t0: 'line:N.start'`) or an action. Each next shot a clearly different angle or size.
3. Characters fully in or fully out of the frame, never half a face at the edge.
4. Actions the story needs happen ON screen, never inside a cut: hand-overs, sitting, a prop opening, an arrival. Start the shot
   at least .3 s before the action.
5. Continuity: no face key, clip start or turn within 3 frames of a cut.
6. Characters big: head 300-430 px wide on talking shots, one establishing wide (180-250 px) per place.
7. Low: camera between the subject's chest and eyes, looking slightly up. Never from above.
8. The camera always moves: a `push` 8-12 % closer over the shot, an `orbit` 10-20 degrees, a `follow` on a walker. A `park` drifts
   slowly by itself; `still: true` on a shot for a real dead-still beat.
9. Dutch roll 1-5 degrees on most shots, drifting a degree over the shot.
10. Foreground depth: a set piece low in the near third, or two people staggered in depth, or over the shoulder.

## Framing numbers (1080x1920; a wide project: `wide.md`)
Head px = `4160 / distance` at fov 26 (`3580 / distance` at fov 30): 300 px = 14 D away. The frame is only `0.26 x distance` D wide at
fov 26, so a two-shot must stack depth (one nearer, heads at 30 % and 70 %) or keep the pair within ~1.9 D. Three in one shot: heads
250+, staggered, ~14-16 D at fov 26-28. Solo: head centre 35-65 % across, 34-50 % down.

## The `path` camera (one continuous move through keys)
```js
{ t0: 0, t1: 99, camera: { move: 'path', keys: [
  { t: 0,   pos: { whos: ['cal', 'maya'], offset: [0.3, 2.6, 8.5] }, target: { whos: ['cal', 'maya'], offset: [0, 2.6, 0] }, fov: 30 },
  { t: 2.3, pos: { who: 'maya', offset: [-0.6, 2.65, 7.0] }, target: { who: 'maya', offset: [0, 2.75, 0] }, fov: 30 },
  { t: 'line:3.start', pos: [1.3, 4.25, 1.2], target: [0.15, 2.4, -10], fov: 38, stop: true } ] } }
```
Monotone cubic per channel: passes every key, no overshoot. `stop: true` = speed zero at that key (an aim that lands after a whip).
`shake` 1 calm, 2 a jolt, 3 panic, .5 holding breath; `walk` 0-1 = the bob of whoever holds the camera.
Keys on a moving thing: `{ object: 'sub', offset: [22, 6, -9] }` (a set object by `.name` or `set.points`; `local: true` turns the
offset with it), `{ prop: 'id', offset }`. A name that does not exist stops the film before anything renders.
- **Whip:** two keys 5-7 frames apart, a key half way aimed sideways (a target passing through the camera has no direction).
- **Over heads:** pass at least 1 D from any head, or the frame goes solid for a few frames. Or stay 4+ D out.
- **Flights:** never look ahead at blank wall; keep the next subject in frame, swing to the face on landing.
- **Long lens + doorway:** aim from the subject through a point just inside the door and put the camera on that line.
- **After everyone turns,** a camera on the old side sees backs: move the peek to the beat when they face it.

## Seams: crossing between places without a visible cut
Places sit 400 D apart (sets.md). A hidden cut is two `path` shots whose last and first frames look alike (`seam: true` on the second):
- **Forward into a surface:** fly at a wall or hull until it fills the frame, cut, come out of another wall still moving. Keep the
  camera outside the shell on the last frame.
- **Backward through a wall:** one frame pops from the room to the outside; at speed it reads as passing through.
- **Water surface:** backward out through it looking down reads well; forward through a bright plane is a flash.
- **Swish:** the same sky in both places, turning the same way on both sides of the cut.
- **Ride a moving thing:** keys on `{ object }` carry the camera with it.
- Keep each crossing under 8 frames (5 dark frames read as passing through, 8 is too long). Land on the next face on the word.
- Hard cut where the hit is stronger than a glide: a jolt, a scream, a reveal.

## Shapes that need care in 9:16 (a wide project: `wide.md`)
A long thing (a ship, a train) reads only from near its axis (within ~10 degrees); from the side it is a wall. Two heads closer than a
helmet cannot be separated by any camera: move the character and say so. Lead a walker from the side he walks towards.

## Review on strips
- `film_sheet` of the whole film: the cut rhythm, faces in every shot, nothing growing out of heads.
- `film_sheet` with `strip` on every fast move and every seam: full frame rate. A camera through a head showed on one frame that
  every-3rd-frame sheets nearly hid.
- `render_frames` on the first frame of each shot and on actions: framing and faces at full size.
- Move the sound cues tied to cuts if the new camera moved the cuts (a whoosh belongs on the whip, not where the old cut was).
# Sets: writing `scenes/set.js`

Units are D (one head). Ground y = 0, the camera side is +Z. An adult's head top is ~2.6-2.8 D, the waist ~1.2, a seat .55, a counter
1.25, a door 3.2 x 1.6. Keep the action in x -6..6, z -2..3 for a single place.

## Three ways to get a set
1. **A kit set by name** (`world: { set: 'park' }`): `bread_corner`, `workshop_yard`, `harbour_pier`, `park`, `kitchen`,
   `city_street`, `plain`. Lit, sun shadows, marks (park `sit` `sit2` `bench_front` `a` `b` `tree` ...; kitchen `counter` `stove`
   `fridge` `stool_l` `stool_r` ...). Marks are only read by name in `sit_on.seat`: write their numbers into `at` and walk paths.
   Details and marks: `world/WORLD_API.md` in the engine copy.
2. **A description object** (`world: { set: { sky, sun, ground, walls, boxes, counters, tables, lamps, trees, marks, ... } }`), built
   by the same kit. Good for a simple place in Build (it still needs its depth and practicals: `references/topics.md`).
3. **Your own `scenes/set.js`** (`world: { set: 'own' }`). Needed for many places, a Blender set, lights as data, post and shading.

## The set module
```js
import { createLightRig } from '../world/look/lights.js';
import { createPost } from '../world/look/post.js';
import { createRigShade } from '../world/look/rigshade.js';
export async function buildSet(THREE, scene, opts, kit) {     // opts = world.setOpts
  const base = kit('plain', opts);                             // optional: start from a kit set name or a description object
  const sub = new THREE.Group(); sub.name = 'sub'; base.group.add(sub);   // .name = what a camera key { object: 'sub' } follows
  const rig = createLightRig(THREE, PLACES, drivers);          // lights as data (below)
  const look = opts.post ? createPost(THREE, rig, opts.post) : undefined;              // the post pass
  if (look && opts.post.shade) look.shading = createRigShade(THREE, rig, opts.post.shade); // the shading pass
  return { ...base, marks: { ...base.marks, door: [2, 1] }, points: { sub }, rig, look,
           update(t) { base.update?.(t); rig.update(t); sub.position.y = 44 - t; } };    // update: pure in t
}
```
It may return as little as `{ group }`. Also: `ready` (a promise: loading done), `lightDir` (direction TO the sun), `casters`
(meshes that cast the sun shadow), `bounds`. Import from the engine copy by relative path (`'../world/look/...'`); load project
files with `new URL('../assets/set/', import.meta.url)`. Everything must fall back to a plain previz when a file is missing, so the
film always renders while the environment crew works.

## Many places in one film
- Each place sits 400 D from the others (`[0, 0]`, `[400, 0]`, `[400, -400]`, `[-400, 0]` ...), inside its own sky dome and its own
  fog, so a cut or a seam between them is free and no place sees another.
- **Domes must write depth** (`depthWrite: true`, `renderOrder: -10`), or other places' domes show through the sky as faint arcs.
- A character goes between places with `acts.<id>.place` keys on cuts, not cast copies.
- Characters in another place cost nothing per frame; extra places do not slow the film, so give every beat the place it needs.
- Moving things (a ship, a sub, a lift) are their own named groups, animated in `update(t)` from numbers the film passes in
  `setOpts` (one table of times in film.js drives the set, the acting and the camera).

## Lights as data (`world/look/lights.js`)
A place: `{ sky: [r,g,b], ground: [r,g,b], fog: { color: '#hex', density: .03 }, ao: { floor: 0, h: 1.6, amt: .45 }, lights: [...],
states: [{ from: 34.06, sky, fog, lights: { id: { power, color } } }] }` (linear colours; `states` = later values from a time on,
put them on a cut). A light: `{ id, kind: 'point' | 'spot' | 'sun', color, power, pos, dir, fall: .05, range: 30, cone: [in, out],
wrap: .2, gobo: { kind: 'cage' | 'caustic', ... }, drive: 'name', move: 'name' }`. `drive` / `move` read functions of t from the set's
`drivers` (a dying lamp, a swinging bulb), so the light stays pure in t. At most 8 lights per place.
`rig.uniforms(place)` = the uniform block for that place's materials; `rig.update(t)` sets the frame; `rig.at(place)` and
`rig.sample(place, t)` are what post and shading read. A one-line light change and a re-render is the fastest look tweak there is.
A gobo (a lamp cage's shadow, a swing from the film's jolt times) sells a light without showing it.

## Surfaces (`world/look/rigkit.js`)
`const K = createKit(THREE, rig, { shadow: base.uniforms, group })` gives `K.surface(place, colour, { map, tile, uv, bump, gloss,
spec, wet, grime, emit, ao, near })`, `K.water(place, ...)`, `K.sky(x, z, r, { top, hor, low })`, `K.decals(place, list, tex)`,
`K.sprites(...)`, and `loadSpriteDefs(THREE, dir)`. `near` dissolves small kit right at the lens (rivets as dark blobs on a flight).
Read the module's header comments for the exact options.

## Rules that cost time before
- Nothing tall right behind where a head will be; nothing thin ending at a head.
- Keep walking lanes, doorways and camera flight lines clear (the layout is a contract once cameras exist).
- A detail pass never moves a wall.
- `update(t)` never keeps state from the previous frame.
# Pitfalls: every trap that cost our runs a re-render, and the fix

From the S-4 short (39 s, five passes) and the backrooms short (base build, four cameras, detail, sprites, shading). One line each: the trap, then the fix.
Paths are the project's: `scenes/film.js`, `scenes/set.js`, `scenes/props/`, `scenes/cast/`, `scenes/post.js`, `scenes/shade.js`, `assets/`, `blender/build_set.py`.
The engine copy (`engine/`, `world/`, `lib/`, `specs/` ...) is read-only: anything below that needs an engine change is a gap to report, not a file to edit.

## Build (characters, acting, basic scene)
- `audio/clean.wav` + `audio/clean.json` are the app's: never trim or edit them. The transcript is the truth for what is said; if it differs from the script ("fights its way"), say so in the report, never fix it silently.
- A film driven by a schedule (knocks, hits, signals): write `scenes/film.js` with ONE table that makes the hands, the visible effects and the timing agree. Hand-written JSON drifts.
- A clip's `at` is read only as a `line:` string. A number in `at` is dropped silently and the clip starts SETTLED on frame 0. Seconds go in `t0`.
- Never open on an empty scene or on a face from behind: open on a face. gruss calls anything else "a bad hook".
- Start everyone turned toward the camera side (|ry| <= 70). Past about 95 deg from the camera the face, beard and glasses vanish and the head is only hair.
- Narrator films: mouths move only on quoted lines, for the person on screen. A voice from off screen is a line with `who: null`.
- A character who must never blink (the backrooms twist): `blink: false` and `listen: []` on her acts, then check her eyes frame by frame in a strip.
- First pass failures the fresh-eyes review found: bodies standing like posts, arms hanging, nobody really running, a grab that is a pose swap. Fix: one body pose change per shot tied to a word, anticipation and settle on every action, runners lean 20-30 deg with a real stride.
- Every arm move needs an end: `hold` + `out`, a later clip on that hand, or a hand-over. An open `point` stays up for good.
- The first strike of a run needs `rise` 6-8 frames, or the hand jumps from hang to ready in one frame (the PROP GUARD caught a 259 px pop).
- An impact is not a teleport: a `knock` marks its own blow, a clip entry takes `snap`, a prop key `snap: true`, a seam shot `hard: true`. Never just switch the guard off: it hides real pops too.
- Give every `drop` key a `from`. Without it the prop starts from where it was, which depends on earlier frames and breaks out-of-order renders.
- A prop that hides itself shows again: the stage sets the prop's own `visible` every frame. Hide an inner group instead (`knockfx.js` does this).
- Many places in one film: one `scenes/set.js` with places 400 D apart, each in its own dome and fog. Domes must write depth, or the other places' domes show through the sky as faint arcs.
- Anything in a place is in every shot of that place: waiting characters, landing dust, a second copy of a diver. Limit effects in time (dust 1.25 s) and keep people out of each other's shots.
- One person in two

err: places: `acts.<id>.place`, not cast copies. Floating, sinking, standing on a deck: `acts.<id>.height`. Nothing collides: a deck is the height you write.
- A follow camera's `camOffset` is in world axes: it ended inside the hull. Use a `path` with the clearance worked out.
- Sand went mint: light power and a bright texture clipped. Lower the light, never fix it in the grade.
- A walker faces his walk direction until the walk ends (`face` lands only at the end): lead him from the side he walks toward.
- Two heads closer than a helmet (about 1.1 D) can't be separated by any camera: move one character and say so.
- Captions sat on the grab hand and the collar at the key moments: check the caption band against the action in the sheet.
- The sound library had no struck steel, sonar or sea. The app does the sound design: make a story sound VISIBLE (impact rings on every knock) so the beat reads either way, and name the missing sound in the report.

## Camera
- Camera styles are instruction sets, not presets: take the logic of Dread Cuts / One Take / Found Footage / The Watcher / Through the Steel, never their coordinates.
- Find what crosses the walls in the story (a sound, a signal) and let the camera travel with it. That one idea made Through the Steel.
- A hidden seam = two `path` shots whose last and first frames look alike: forward into steel until it fills the frame, out of another wall still moving; keep the camera outside the shell on the last frame (inside it you see the far wall).
- Backward through a wall: one frame pops from room to plate and reads as passing through at speed. Forward through a bright water plane = a white flash; backward out through it looking down reads well.
- Swish: same sky and water in both places, turning the same way on both sides of the cut.
- Keep each crossing under 8 frames: 8 dark steel frames read as a stall, 5 read as passing through.
- Riding a falling thing: a `path` key `pos: { object: "sub", offset: [...] }` (the set names the object or lists it in `points`), or keys computed every 0.1 s from the set's own motion formula.
- 9:16 and anything long (a ship): only a frame within about 10 deg of its axis says "ship". From the side it is a grey wall at any distance.
- Aim wides at where a moving thing really is at that time (the cutter was 14 D back until 6.69 s, so the first wide framed water).
- A camera flew through a head and the every-3rd-frame preview nearly hid it: check every flight with `film_sheet {strip: 'A-B'}` at full frame rate.
- Frame 0 must be clean: moving closer wasn't enough (an edge head appeared); parallax fixed it (camera to the side, aim kept on the subject).
- The camera floor raises a low `push`/`park`/`follow` to the nearest chest, which ruins a wide of a ship (`lowCam: true`). `path` shots are never raised.
- Locked-off shots read dead: every shot moves, even 2-4 % of scale or 30-60 px of travel.
- One Take: with no cuts nothing hides a change, so ease moods in and out, clear sprites along the flight (`sprites.clearPath`), raise the path over heads it would pass through, and hide what comes too near the lens (`look.hideNearPx`).
- The automatic sound design ties cues to cuts: after a new camera, tell the member to re-run it in the app.
- **A solid ink-coloured frame for 1-6 frames = a character BESIDE the camera's image plane** (depth about zero from the lens,
  anywhere sideways, even far outside the frame): a camera inside a ring of people, a push that crosses someone's depth, a macro
  inside a crowd. Keep every character clearly in front of or behind the lens plane on every frame (a long lens from outside the
  ring). The Town film lost two passes to guessing other causes.
- A camera looking UP sees none of the place (its frame bottom above the horizon): dress that camera's frame by screen position
  (roofs, a lamp post, branches placed where its frame is), or move it.

## Environment (Blender set, Flow textures, live light)
- Read what the camera sees FIRST: portrait at fov 26 is a slit (about 1.4 D either side of the subject; a wide project sees about 4 times that, `wide.md`). The back wall and the overhead are the set; model those first.
- Read every camera key against the geometry before placing anything: flights end inside walls, climb through ceilings, look straight down. Leave their slots open.
- Take character positions and walks from `scenes/film.js`, not from the old set: a walk found late had a torn sheet sitting on it.
- Write down the handedness per place: looking along +z, +x is frame LEFT. Gear went on the wrong side once.
- Fix the contract up front: decal cell ranges (Blender and Flow numbered them differently), glbs are place-local, one glb per moving thing placed inside its animated group, agreed material names (an unknown name means nothing to the loader).
- A painted pattern has a period and a phase: modelled rivets fought painted ones. Six strakes, each exactly one texture plate wide, with the modelled lap on the painted seam.
- Nothing thin may end at a head: a hose behind the Navy man read as an aerial growing out of him. Cut those triangles in `scenes/set.js` if the glb has them.
- Check in clay at the real shot times, on a tiled sheet with capsules for people (`blender_run` + `tex_job {kind: 'sheet'}`). Numbers can't see "behind a face"; the clay found the davit wire, the boom, the ladder and foreground rocks.
- Growth along plate laps lined up as lumps: noise patches only. Sand ripples looked like corduroy: warp them and let them come and go. Flat-shaded boulders looked like gems: smooth them.
- Decals on curves: keep them under about 1.4 D along the curve (sagitta = s^2 / (8 r)), or the ends sink or float.
- A Blender error can hide in a long log: look for `Traceback`, `Error`, `File "` in what `blender_run` returns.
- Flow makes about 1 picture per 2 min with misses. Ask for few pictures, priority order first, and anything that ends the film (the dawn) near the top.
- A Flow policy block is not always the words: retry once; after two blocks, change the words ("diamond tread" blocked six times, "raised ridges" passed).
- Prompts for tiling textures: "straight top-down scan, very low contrast, evenly lit" plus a list of no's (stains, creases, shadows, perspective, text). Any feature repeats and gives the tile away; damage goes in decals.
- Decals darken, never tint, and their alpha reaches zero well inside the cell, or a square edge shows.
- Look at every raw sprite sheet: an extra object drawn shifted every name after it, with no error. Mark the extra `"skip": true`; a grid fallback means the sheet is wrong.
- Numbers don't prove a wrap on large soft pictures (a sky passed the seam number and still showed an edge): look at 3 x 3 tilings in the `tex_job` previews.
- A bad picture went live for 50 s while the preview was loading: write new recipes to a preview name first.
- Textures rewritten while the preview loads them: the page loads them once at its start. Wait for `assets/tex/` to go quiet before the final render.
- Anything that lands after the lights are tuned (the storm sky) can be far too bright in this grade: re-check it.
- Never tint a whole ceiling tile: it reads as a patchwork. Mask stains inside the tile.
- An important silhouette went brown in the haze: keep a clear column around it (`thingClear`).
- Modelled rivets near the lens became dark hexagons: dissolve small kit near the camera; hide what grows outside a hull while the camera is inside it.
- A caustic gobo projected on walls smears into streaks: limit it to surfaces that face up.
- A label in murk needs emit well over 1 to survive fog at 30 D.
- The place lights cast no real shadows on the set (a known gap): a gobo (cage shadow, swinging from the film's jolt times) sells the lamp instead.
- Sprites looked modest on stills and were "HUGE IMPROVEMENT" in motion: judge them moving, place them where the camera sees them, never right behind a face.
- Render the whole film early for a safe result, and again when late files land.
- **Never pink, lilac or purple on a magenta sprite sheet:** the key reads them as half background, they come out muddy and
  see-through, and `tex_job check` still says OK. Say "nothing pink, nothing purple, nothing magenta on any object" and name the
  colours instead (peach-orange, white, mint, teal, sky blue). "A pair of shutters" came as TWO objects: ask for "one single shutter".
- Colours set with `color.setRGB()` are linear, hex strings are sRGB: a night tint of .5 comes out pale (.73 on screen).
- A transparent overlay drawn with `depthTest: false` veils the characters (transparent things draw after everything opaque): only
  opaque domes may skip the depth test.
- Ring pieces around a centre: local x is the tangent at `ry = t`, not `t + 90 deg`, or every kerb stone turns into a spoke. The clay
  picture showed it at once; the numbers did not.
- The Blender track ships the pieces most shots see first (houses, walls), each as soon as it passes its clay check: pieces that land
  after the integration's first round stay previz boxes in that round.

## Post processing
- Start from the last approved settings, then tune: the backrooms values got the torpedo room to the bar on the first render.
- Compare sheets catch what single frames hide: the milky water looked lovely alone and lost the submarine. The story's subject wins: haze density keys per shot.
- Water: light that fades from the real surface height (`top`), shafts with a period around 15 D. Shafts of 6 D average out to nothing along the ray.
- Particles are quads and capsules, not points (points clip whole at the frame edge and can't streak).
- Keep a streak's width out of the blur size (`cocK`), or sleet turns to confetti.
- Bubbles have no shutter (a streaked bubble is a pill) and need `nearFade` 1.6..4, or they read as wire rings near the lens.
- Burst `size` and `grow` are per-second numbers: a soft puff at the ram whited out the frame. Tune a burst one frame after the hit, by eye.
- Spray behind a wall is invisible: put `at` between the people and the wall; the depth test keeps it off faces.
- Sun in haze: phase `g` .55, not .72, or the dawn goes pure white.
- A material in `scenes/set.js` that writes display colour (bulb, halo, water surface) can go dark with post on: check them on a before/after sheet.
- Grain tripled the file size: leave it out unless asked.
- **The dark-interior numbers on a bright exterior make a grey-white veil** (the Town film): haze `far` 220 put full haze over the
  sky and turned it white, aperture 26 blurred the story prop in the foreground, glow lights at power 60-120 whited out the night.
  It ended at about half the haze, `far` 70-90, aperture 9, glow power .85-4. Start from the matching row of quality-bar.md.
- `air: { density: 0 }` without its other keys is not "off": leave `air` out of a place to switch it off.
- Every settings place in `scenes/post.js` needs a rig place of the same name (the particles read its lights), or the film throws
  "Cannot read properties of undefined".

## Shading
- Key and shadow as two colours (warm on the lamp side, cold on the far side) is most of the pass.
- A constant cold film light makes the room colder by itself as the lamp dies: let the light's physics carry the story.
- A floor per place (`floor`, `keyMin`) stops mud, and must allow for the grade after it (a dark place with gamma .62 needs numbers that look far too high).
- A dying light loses its colour; it doesn't stay orange: a warm `keyMin` turned the kid brown. Near neutral (about .66 .6 .52).
- Metal keeps its own colour: brass in teal light went acid green. `metal.keep` .62 desaturates the light on metal only.
- Faces went saturated cyan underwater: `sat` .62, a higher floor.
- A dim key with a stronger fill turned the drawn shadow inside out: cap the fill under the key.
- Hats shade with the head, with no rim (the rim drew arcs across caps).
- Rings, flashes and impact stars are light: never shade them.
- Props keep only the sharp highlight: flat wrench heads became cream lollipops.
- Backlit (dawn): the face is all shadow side, so the shadow side carries the warmth.
- Before fixing something odd, check the earlier pass: a "shading bug" on the skipper was his drawn hair.
- Flicker ("like if it's clipping"): light direction ignores flicker (`noSteer`), power read over about +-.4 s, position over +-.24 s along the character's own timeline, level over +-.1 s, and `steps` at every hard change of light, which sits on a cut.
- Keep each character in one place: then a hidden cut has nothing to pop.
- Run `film_check {kind: 'shade_jumps'}` after tuning, not during: it takes as long as a render. Camera whips move the shade; that is accepted.

## Review and tools
- Look at moving footage: `film_sheet` (the whole film tiled) after every change, `strip: 'A-B'` at full rate on fast moves and actions, `cuts` around every cut. Stills undersell and hide flicker.
- Judge new looks on before/after sheets of the same frames, with the final grade on: the grade changes everything.
- Send back a short ranked list of radical fixes, never many micro notes.
- After each pass, `film_check {kind: 'same'}`: characters, props and shots unchanged (the shots only change in Camera angles).
- `film_probe` after changes to props, hands or shots: read the PROP GUARD line. Framing (a head at the edge, behind the camera, two
  heads overlapping) has no number in the app: look at each shot's first frame with `render_frames` and the cuts with `film_sheet { cuts: true }`.
