- A frame is not bit-exact between renders (a few pixels differ): compare to a tolerance, never byte for byte.
- A failed render prints a stack trace whose real line is far above the tail: read the whole error.
- Small flaws next to the bar (pale frames at a water surface, a weak spray): fix them when your step touches that moment; report each one you leave in one line.
- Say exactly what you did not check (sound is the app's, nobody listened).

## Performance
- A 39 s film renders in about 2 minutes (70-90 ms a frame): a whole-film `film_sheet` per round beats choosing frames.
- Character CPU work is most of a frame, not the set: many places, sprites, post and shading cost close to nothing measurable.
- A character outside both the camera and the sun's shadow camera is skipped. A huge character or one carrying a big prop may pop at the frame edge: report it (the cull radius is in the engine).
- `quality: 'auto'` gives the preview setting below 1200 px on the long side, so the live preview stays smooth; never force `full` in the preview.
- ms per frame on a sparse spread of frames is misleading (page load spread over few frames): compare consecutive ranges or full renders.
# Step: Build

**Goal:** turn the member's voice into a film where cartoon characters act every line so well they feel alive, in a lit set with
DEPTH, opening on a character's scared or expressive face. Characters and acting are the heart of it: "perfect character
animation" from a blank script or any character. The set is the previz (the rich set is the Environment overhaul) but it has
depth from the start: the later passes can only add detail and air to the space you give them, and a set that is a wall right
behind the faces stays flat forever.

**Inputs:** `audio/clean.wav` + `audio/clean.json` (the voice and its word times, made by the app), the member's notes, the engine
copy. A SHOT PLAN (binding) in the notes, when there is one, fixes the cuts, places and cameras: follow it segment for segment.

**The bar:** `references/quality-bar.md` and the stills in `references/bar/` (open them first): the space behind the faces, the
practical lights, the faces big. **The guide pages** (`references/guide/`, open the jpg files): 01 the bar, 02 story to shots
(before any scene), 03 the set, 04 characters, 05 the camera grammar, 09 verify, 10 never. Read them before you start and check
your frames against them before you finish. When the project has `references/examples/`, its Build sections show how the bar films
started.

**Made new:** the examples show the method; this film is written from this voice's own words. Never copy an example's film,
acting table, shots, camera or set, even when the voice is the same as an example's: its own cast, its own set in `scenes/set.js`
(or a kit set), its own acting.

**Wide project (16:9):** read `references/wide.md` first. Stage for the width from the first shot and give the set its sides; the rest of this step holds as written.

## Read first
`SKILL.md`, `references/topics.md`, `references/critic.md`, `references/quality-bar.md` (and open the stills in

`references/bar/`), `references/voice-sound.md`, `references/characters.md`, `references/film.md`, `references/camera.md` (the
grammar section), `references/sets.md`, the Build part of `references/pitfalls.md`, and `lessons/build.md` if it exists. Deep
names: `references/api/`.

## Method
1. **Words and the film bible:** read `narration` (or `audio/clean.json`) from 0 to the end. Write the lines as heard (note
   anything that differs from the member's script). Then `scenes/BIBLE.md` by `references/topics.md`: a row per line (speaker,
   place, beat, action word, story prop) and a row per place (the real thing, size in D, far end in D, practicals, colour mood,
   air). Decide everything here first.
2. **Cast:** who says each line, who is the narrator, who else is in the scene. A spec per character in `scenes/cast/<id>.json`
   from a sentence each (or a built-in spec by id). Check each new one on a `render_frames` frame facing the camera and at 3/4.
3. **Set with depth:** the places of the bible in `scenes/set.js` (several places 400 D apart, lights as data, the later passes
   build on it). Each place: the far end 25 D or more from the camera with the camera looking along it, so most shots have space
   behind the characters (a vanishing point helps); 2 or more practicals you can see (lamps, panels, a window) placed along that
   depth. Stage the characters in the space, not against its wall. Keep walking lanes and the camera side clear.
4. **Prove the opening first:** stage, act and light the first shot (the face, the place behind it, its practicals), then run
   the opening critic round (`references/critic.md`) and fix what it names before you act the rest.
5. **Acting:** for every line, the speaker AND the listeners: face first, one body action tied to a word, dead-still holds,
   looks, reactions. Props with owners and hand-overs. Walks that end before the line that needs them.
6. **Camera:** the grammar (camera.md): on the speaker, a cut every 1.5-3 s on a word, low, always moving, faces big. Frame 0 = a face.
7. **Review loop:** `check_preview` -> `film_probe` (shots, PROP GUARD) -> `film_sheet` of the whole film -> `render_frames` on
   faces, actions, feet on the floor and hands on props -> fix the worst thing -> again. Strips on anything fast.
8. **Critic rounds** on the whole film (`references/critic.md`) until the exit list below is true and a critic says YES.
9. **Lessons:** `lessons/build.md` as you go (tried, saw, fixed, still weak), ending with the HANDOVER block (`references/review.md`).

Helper agents for clearly separate jobs (one character's spec, one group's acting, the set) are welcome: each gets the helper
contract of `references/critic.md`, owns its own files, runs in the foreground; `scenes/film.js` stays yours.

## Machine checks
`check_preview` (no load, runtime or film error), `film_probe` (every line and word, PROP GUARD over every frame),
`film_check { kind: 'set' }` (measured and written into the HANDOVER: the Environment overhaul must pass it, Build may not).

## Exit (every line true)
- `scenes/BIBLE.md` is complete (`references/topics.md` section 8).
- The first frame shows a readable, expressive face (head 300 px wide or more on 9:16; `references/wide.md` on 16:9). Talking
  shots: heads 300-430 px; one establishing wide per place: 180-250 px.
- Every word in `audio/clean.json` is in a line, as heard. `check_preview` clean, `film_probe` PROP GUARD passes.
- Every line has its speaker's face key and one tied action; listeners react 1-3 frames after the trigger word.
- Cuts every 1.5-3 s on a line start or an action; each shot a clearly different angle or size; no face key, clip start or
  turn within 3 frames of a cut.
- No face cut by the frame edge, nothing growing out of a head, no back on a speaker, feet on the floor.
- In 3 of every 4 shots or more, space behind the faces (no blank wall within a few D filling the background); every place has
  2+ visible light sources. Looked at with `render_frames` at `scale: 1` next to the bar stills.
- The opening critic round and the final critic round answered YES with no BLOCKING fault.
- `lessons/build.md` ends with its HANDOVER, including the set bar numbers.

## Never
A back or an empty set in the first frame; a wall a metre behind the faces "for now"; a beat, a line or a character left out
to finish; anything copied from an example.

## Report
Two or three lines: what you made, what differs from the script, what is weakest (the HANDOVER's first open item).

## Runner-owned prop and probe contract
Write `props.json` as `{ "props": [{ "name": "…", "appearsAt": 0.1, "cropBox": { "x": 0, "y": 0, "w": 0.1, "h": 0.1 } }], "setDressing": ["…"] }`. Keep key props separate from set dressing. Seed `setDressing` with the visible architectural basics and set pieces that actually occur (for example wall, floor, ceiling, counter, table); do not allow objects that are absent. Every declared prop needs a normalized cropBox aimed at the current probe composition. If you change camera/framing, re-aim every prop cropBox before the runner's next gate. The program renders probes under `out/passes/build/probe-*.png`; inspect prior-round files when available. Never run `heart still`, start a local server, or invoke a command that starts a server. The pass runner owns still rendering; this builder seat cannot bind local ports.
# Wide films (16:9, 1920x1080)

A project made as Wide 16:9 is 1920x1080 everywhere: preview, `render_frames`, `film_sheet`, every check, the export. The project's
format decides; write `size: [1920, 1080]` in `scenes/film.js` so the file says the same. Same five passes, same method, same bar.
Only the framing changes. Where another file gives px numbers for 1080x1920 or talks about a tall frame or a "slit", this file wins.

## What the frame does
fov is the VERTICAL lens, so the same camera at the same distance shows the same height of the world, and about three times the width.

| at fov 26 | tall (1080x1920) | wide (1920x1080) |
|---|---|---|
| head size | `4160 / distance` px | `2340 / distance` px (`2015 / distance` at fov 30) |
| head as a share of frame height | the same | the same |
| frame width at the subject | `0.26 x distance` D | `0.82 x distance` D |
| either side of a subject 14 D away | about 1.8 D | about 5.7 D |

Px numbers here are real pixels of the 1920x1080 frame: measure heads on `render_frames` at `scale: 1`.

## Framing numbers
- Talking shot: head 220-340 px (7-11 D away at fov 26). Close-up on a reaction: up to 450 px, the head off centre.
- A place's establishing shot: head 110-160 px (15-21 D).
- Solo: head centre at a third of the width (about 33 % or 67 %), 30-45 % down, looking INTO the empty side. Dead centre only when
  the shot is about being trapped or confronted.
- Two people: side by side now works. Heads at about 30 % and 70 %, 3-5 D apart, 10-13 D away, or staggered in depth when one matters
  more. No need to stack them as a tall frame must.
- Three or more: spread them across the width at different depths, heads 180+ px. Nobody's head cut by the frame edge: with this much
  width a half face at the edge is an accident, not a crop. Check the edges of every group shot.
- Captions sit low in a wide frame (words at 80 %, full lines at 86 % of the height, sized on the height). Keep every speaking face
  above about 72 %, and the feet can go under the words.

## Use the width (this is what wide is for)
- **Something in the empty side:** the thing they fear, the person they are talking about, a window, a door. An empty third with a
  reason is the strongest wide picture; an empty third with nothing in it is a shot framed too loosely.
- **Near things on one side:** a pipe, a door edge or a shoulder dark and soft on the left or right third, the subject on the other.
- **Sideways moves read now:** a track alongside a walker, a slide from one speaker to the next without a cut. Lead a walker with
  the room in front of him.
- **Depth still comes first.** Wide is not flat: the camera still looks along the set's depth, low, with space and light behind the
  faces. Do not line people up against a wall because they now fit.
- Long things (a ship, a train, a table of people) can be shown side-on from far enough away; a tall frame could not.

## The set must be wide too
A tall frame hid everything beyond about 1.5 D either side of the subject; here both sides of the set are on screen. So:
- Read `film_probe` shots and work out what each camera sees sideways, not only behind the face. Full width of a shot at distance
  `d` is `0.82 x d` D: a back wall 20 D behind a subject the camera is 10 D from shows about 25 D of wall.
- No edge of the world in frame: side walls or dressing on both sides of every place, floor and ceiling wide enough, the far end
  wider than you would build it for a tall film. A set that ends shows as a hard edge or a void; look at the frame edges.
- Practical lights and big shapes spread ACROSS the width as well as along the depth, so the sides are not dark and empty.
- Detail goes where the eye goes, and that is now the left and right thirds as well as the middle. Plan about three times the visible
  surface: model and dress what the cameras really see, leave what they never see.
- Backgrounds and full-frame pictures: `make_picture` with aspect 16:9. Wide plates for what is seen through windows and doors, since
  much more of them shows.
- Blender: `blender_run { script: 'blender/check_set.py', args: ['--wide', '--render', '2.1', '14'] }`: the camera samples and the clay
  pictures use the 16:9 frame (check_set_template.py).

## Each pass
- **Build:** stage for the width from the first shot (the thirds, the two-shots above). Frame 0 is still a face. Build a set with sides.
- **Camera angles:** the instruction set's feel and logic stay; only the composition changes. Below.
- **Environment overhaul:** the crew's contract says the frame is 16:9. Keep-clear zones and flight lines are the same; the sides of
  each place join the list of what each shot must show. Tell every agent in its brief: "wide film, read references/wide.md".
- **Add post processing:** haze, depth of field, bloom and grade work as they are (`maxBlur` scales with the frame height). Check
  particles and dust reach the sides: a dust `box` made for a tall frame is too narrow, so widen it across the camera and raise the
  count by the same factor. A vignette reads stronger on the far left and right: judge it on the sides.
- **Shading pass:** nothing changes in the method. Characters now often stand at the sides of the frame, so check faces at the edges.

## The five camera sets in a wide frame
| set | same as ever | wide |
|---|---|---|
| Dread Cuts | hard cuts on the words, low, tilted, a push on every shot | put the dread in the empty side: a figure on one third, the dark or the door on the other. Change the side on each cut, as the roll does. |
| One Take | one unbroken path, flights landing on words | long sideways slides between speakers read beautifully. On flights both sides of the path are seen: check strips for set edges and void, and clear sprites a wider lane. |
| Found Footage | a person with a phone, fov 46, shake, whips | held sideways it shows a lot: 4-5 D from a face now also shows who stands beside them. Whips travel further, so land them with a `stop`. Use a narrower fov (35-40) if the sides of the set run out. |
| The Watcher | a long lens from far away, level, creeping | fov 9-16 from 15-25 D. A door frame or corner can fill a whole third as the hiding place. Hold people small at one side when the silence wants it, end tight on a face. |
| Through the Steel | the camera travels with what crosses the walls, seams under 8 frames | seams must fill the WHOLE width: fly closer into the wall or hull than you would in a tall frame, or the edge of it shows at the sides. Close on faces between crossings. |

## Review
`film_sheet` tiles are wide (fewer columns, more rows); `strip` and `cuts` as ever. The bar stills in `references/bar/` are 9:16:
compare faces, light, richness and depth with them, not the shape. At `render_frames` `scale: 1`, look at the left and right edges of
every shot first: that is where a wide film goes wrong.

      { id: 'sun', kind: 'sun', dir: [-0.5, 0.74, 0.45], color: [1.0, 0.95, 0.85], power: 1.0, wrap: 0.3 },

      { id: 'lamp', kind: 'point', pos: [8.2, 6.8, 5.2], color: [1.0, 0.85, 0.6], power: 1.2, fall: 0.05, range: 20, wrap: 0.25 },

function buildDressing() {
  const g = new THREE.Group();
  const wood = flat('#a8784c'), woodDark = flat('#7a5a38');
  const crate = flat('#b08d5a'), leaf = flat('#5a8a4a'), leafDark = flat('#3f6a38');
  const stone = flat('#9a938a'), iron = flat('#3a4a5a');
  const add = (geo, mat, x, y, z, ry = 0, w = 0.02) => {
    const m = part(geo, mat, w);
    m.position.set(x, y, z); m.rotation.y = ry; g.add(m); return m;
  };
  // crates + barrel against the cafe wall (left of the CAFE shopfront)
  add(new THREE.BoxGeometry(0.7, 0.7, 0.7), crate, -5.6, 0.35, -2.55, 0.2);
  add(new THREE.BoxGeometry(0.55, 0.55, 0.55), crate, -4.85, 0.28, -2.6, -0.15);
  add(new THREE.BoxGeometry(0.5, 0.5, 0.5), woodDark, -5.25, 0.95, -2.55, 0.4);
  add(new THREE.CylinderGeometry(0.32, 0.36, 0.85, 14), iron, -3.4, 0.43, -2.6);
  // wooden bench against the wall between the shops
  add(new THREE.BoxGeometry(2.2, 0.12, 0.6), wood, 0.2, 0.55, -2.55);
  add(new THREE.BoxGeometry(0.12, 0.55, 0.55), woodDark, -0.8, 0.28, -2.55);
  add(new THREE.BoxGeometry(0.12, 0.55, 0.55), woodDark, 1.2, 0.28, -2.55);
  add(new THREE.BoxGeometry(2.2, 0.5, 0.1), wood, 0.2, 0.85, -2.8);
  // planters with green crowns along the wall base (right of the bench)
  for (const [x, s] of [[3.6, 1.0], [5.2, 0.8], [-9.5, 0.9]]) {
    add(new THREE.BoxGeometry(0.7 * s, 0.45, 0.5), stone, x, 0.23, -2.6);
    const c = add(new THREE.SphereGeometry(0.42 * s, 12, 10), leaf, x, 0.62, -2.6);
    c.scale.y = 0.75;
    add(new THREE.SphereGeometry(0.3 * s, 10, 8), leafDark, x + 0.25 * s, 0.55, -2.55);
  }
  // street trees at the far ends, crowns above head height
  for (const x of [-12.5, 15.2]) {
    add(new THREE.CylinderGeometry(0.14, 0.2, 2.6, 10), woodDark, x, 1.3, -2.5);
    const c1 = add(new THREE.SphereGeometry(1.1, 12, 10), leaf, x, 3.1, -2.5);
    c1.scale.y = 0.85;
    add(new THREE.SphereGeometry(0.75, 10, 8), leafDark, x + 0.7, 2.7, -2.5);
  }
  g.traverse(m => { m.frustumCulled = false; });
  return g;
}

}
